newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Swiss Novartis shares ease on debut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swiss Novartis shares ease on debut.

text.p: Shares in Novartis, the world number two in pharmaceuticals formed by merging Swiss rivals Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz, eased on their first day of stock market trading on Monday.
Novartis made its debut at 1,502 Swiss francs per registered share, then eased through the day, breaking below 1,490 shortly before the close at 1,488 francs.

This was a 0.4 percent decline from Friday's close for Sandoz, whose shares were swapped one-to-one for Novartis, and in line with an overall easing in the blue-chip Swiss Market Index (SMI) of 0.38 percent.
One Novartis share is worth 1-1/15 Ciba shares, which ended at 1,595 francs on Friday.
Traders said the market. already dulled by very thin pre-Christmas volume, reacted with disappointment late in the day after no major buying of the shares appeared.
"People may have expected more on the first day of trading", one trader said.
Analysts said the price transition from Sandoz and Ciba to Novartis went much as expected with no sudden jumps because it had been planned and prepared for nine months.
"We were expecting a smooth transition like this," Jo Walton at Lehman Brothers said.

Many analysts agree with projections by Novartis of higher profits and lower costs in 1997 based on merger synergies and savings and expect the share price to gain more strongly than the overall SMI next year.
Ciba and Sandoz have estimated the merger would save about two billion francs ($1.5 billion) over three years, including cutting the combined workforce by about 10 percent, or 12,000 jobs.
Forecasts for the Novartis registered share price in 1997 range from 1,650 to 1,750 francs, or 11 to 18 percent above Monday's close.
"Novartis has a strong upside potential," said John Murphy from Goldman Sachs, which does not have a target price for the share.
Goldman Sachs has put Novartis on its priority list for 1997, one of only two shares from about 20 European drug sector companies to achieve the ranking.
"They are looking at strong savings and new products in the pipeline in 1997," Murphy said.
Ciba and Sandoz merged on Friday after long-awaited regulatory approval from the U.S. Federal Trade Commision (FTC) last week cleared the final obstacle.
The fusion created the world's biggest pharmaceutical company after Britain's Glaxo-Wellcome, with a focus on health care, agribusiness and nutrition.
Novartis has 4.4 percent of the world's fragmented pharmaceutical market, based on 1995 sales, while Glaxo-Wellcome had 4.7 percent.

When it was announced last March, the fusion was the world's biggest corporate merger by combined capitalisation, which at that time stood at 75 billion francs ($56 billion). Novartis is now valued at about 105 billion francs.

Novartis would have had sales equivalent to 36 billion francs in 1995 with 3.5 billion spent on research and development. It is a world leader in generic drugs and crop protection and has top positions in several other markets.
Novartis expects a profit of around four billion francs in 1996, while merger costs this year should total two billion.
The merger of Sandoz and Ciba was approved by each company's shareholders in April and by the European Commission in July.
($1=1.3395 Swiss Franc)
